strengths: The paper introduces a novel and well-motivated notion of group fairness for optimal transport: constraining the group-marginal coupling π_SW of a transport plan to match a target F ∈ Π(p, q). This is modular, accommodates a central planner's preferences (quotas, homogamy limits), and fills a genuine gap between individual fairness in matching (Gale–Shapley line of work) and fairness-via-OT for downstream predictions.

The theory is substantive: Proposition 3.3 gives an exact Sinkhorn-like structure for the constrained problem (extra group-level scaling), Theorem 4.2 establishes a 1/√n sample complexity bound for the fairness-penalized entropic OT problem matching the best known rates for unpenalized entropic OT, and Theorem 4.4 provides a uniform-over-Θ deviation bound for the fairness loss of transport plans computed with learned costs, generalizing Rigollet & Strømme. The proofs in the appendix are reasonably detailed and the proof techniques (linearization of the convex penalty, sandwiching, rescaling of dual potentials) are plausible and, to my knowledge, correct in outline.

The two relaxation strategies (convex penalization solved by generalized conditional gradient, and bilevel cost learning) are complementary, and the paper honestly compares their convexity/interpretability/reusability trade-offs rather than overselling one.
The reusability experiment (Figure 7) demonstrating 3–4 orders of magnitude inference-time savings of learned costs over re-solving the penalized problem is a useful practical contribution.
Related work is well surveyed and the paper clearly positions itself against Nguyen et al. (2025), Lobo et al., and constrained OT literature.
weaknesses: Experiments are exclusively on synthetic data (Gaussian mixtures, concentric circles) with very small sample sizes (n = 20 per subgroup, n₀ = 200). The paper motivates the work with school assignment, dating apps, and kidney exchange, but evaluates on none of these or any real dataset, and no baselines from the fair-matching literature (e.g., Lobo et al.) are compared. The empirical significance of the claims is therefore limited.

The convergence claim for FairSinkhorn (Remark 1) is asserted by analogy with alternating projections [4], but the fairness update is a group-level KL-type rescaling, not an orthogonal Euclidean projection; the cited result does not straightforwardly apply, and no convergence rate or proof of the claim for the full algorithm is provided.

Assumption mismatches between statements and proofs: Theorem 4.2 states Assumptions 3.1 and 4.1 (compact support, C^∞ cost), but the proof additionally assumes the cost is L-Lipschitz continuous; this should be in the theorem statement.

Presentation is sloppy in places, undermining confidence: Sections 5.1 and 5.2 are duplicated ('Approaches and Metrics' twice with slightly different text), the appendix contains unresolved citation placeholders ('as proposed in ? ]', 'we found Adam [ ? ]'), the caption of Figure 5 describes circular data as '2D Gaussians', and the Figure 5 legend shows labels (w=0, w=1) inconsistent with the stated three groups.

No error bars or statistical variability are reported; conclusions from plots with ~10-40 points per configuration are hard to assess. The utility metric is restricted to KL divergence to the unconstrained plan and total cost difference; matched-pair quality (e.g., distances of matched individuals), which matters most in matching applications, is not analyzed.

The fairness targets tested are essentially a single family (anti-diagonal targets); the flexibility advertised in the framework is not exercised empirically. The price of fairness is shown only qualitatively.

Reproducibility is uncertain: code 'will be made public upon publication' and is not included; combined with missing hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, independent verification is difficult at review time. There is also no dedicated limitations or research-ethics discussion, which is notable for a paper about enforcing demographic properties in matching systems.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: imposing explicit group-wise mass constraints (fairness targets) on the OT plan itself, which the authors convincingly argue has not been previously considered (prior fairness-OT work uses OT as a tool for downstream prediction). The framework flexibly covers homogamy limits, quotas (four-fifths rule, EU directive), etc.

Clean technical treatment of the exact-fairness problem: the dual characterization (Prop. 3.3) showing the fair plan has Sinkhorn-like form with an extra group-level potential H leads naturally to the FairSinkhorn algorithm, which is a minimal and elegant modification of Sinkhorn-Knopp.

Meaningful theoretical results: a finite-sample O(1/√n) bound for penalized entropic OT matching the rate of standard entropic OT (showing the fairness penalty does not degrade statistical efficiency), and a uniform-over-parameter-family deviation bound for fairness of plans computed with a learned cost on unseen samples, giving a fairness generalization guarantee for the reusability property.

Well-differentiated related work: the paper carefully positions itself against fairness in matching mechanisms (Gale-Shapley variants, kidney exchange), fair bipartite graph matching, fairness-via-OT literature, and constrained/statistical OT, including an extended appendix review.

Exercises include a fairness-cost trade-off analysis, an inference-time/reusability experiment for learned costs, and a deterministic-sampling check (Fig. 7b); code is released and implementation details (solvers, grids, hyperparameters) are given in Appendix D.

Thoughtful impact statement acknowledging that the choice of fairness target is a political/ethical decision rather than something the method prescribes; honest limitations discussion (group fairness only, open fairness-bias trade-off question, downstream outcomes unmodeled).
weaknesses: No convergence analysis for FairSinkhorn: Proposition 3.3 characterizes the optimum but the algorithm's convergence to that optimum (existence/uniqueness of the fixed point of the modified Sinkhorn iteration) is only assessed empirically (Fig. 7a, 'qualitatively similar rates'). This is a significant gap for the paper's headline algorithm.

Theoretical contributions, while correct-looking, are largely extensions of existing machinery (Genevay et al. 2019, Mena & Niles-Weed 2019, Rigollet & Stromme 2025, Rakotomamonjy et al. 2015); the bounds inherit exponential dependence on ε^{-1} and λ (e.g., scaling breaks down when λKsKw ≳ ‖c‖∞/ε), limiting their practical guidance, and constants are hidden behind ≲.

Experimental scale and baselines are limited: synthetic experiments use only 250/25 samples, and the semi-synthetic experiment is a subsampled Kaggle dating dataset with hand-constructed compatibility and cost functions. There is no comparison against alternative approaches for the constrained OT problem (e.g., a general-purpose constrained LP/QP solver, or existing constrained/structured OT methods), so it is hard to assess whether the proposed machinery is practically superior to naive alternatives.

The cost-learning approach is non-convex bilevel optimization with only empirical evidence of success; no analysis of local minima, initialization sensitivity, or when the parametric family can even represent a fair plan (the Mahalanobis family demonstrably cannot reach fairness below 10^-2 on the Circles data).

The relaxation from exact constraints to the penalized objective uses a squared penalty whose solution need not satisfy any prescribed tolerance ρ; the connection between the penalty parameter λ and the actual fairness violation level is only explored empirically, not theoretically.

Presentation issues: several typos and minor errors ('O(1/√n −1)' in Theorem 4.2's formal statement, 'The the cost learning approach', 'a throughout analysis', 'assignements', 'symmetrical arguments', notation switching between Πϵ and Πε), which while not fatal, suggest insufficient proofreading.

The empirical fairness measurement in experiments is with respect to sample-level empirical group frequencies; no experiment probes sensitivity to the assumed fairness target F or to estimation error in group probabilities p, q when they must be estimated from data.
